items.title: Reusable helper modules
items.text: These optional Lua helper modules are available from the shared module root in distributions that include them. They build on the public API; you may also author your own modules. A missing helper is a packaging issue, not permission to use undocumented interfaces.

items.title: ability_executor
items.text:
Continuous rotations should use one top-level executor to retain, poll, replace, and safely cancel a single command:

local AbilityExecutor = require("ability_executor")
local executor = AbilityExecutor.new()

gos.on_tick(function()
  executor:tick()

  if not Settings.active then
    if executor:has_pending() then
      executor:cancel("inactive")
    end
    return
  end

  if not executor:has_pending() and should_cast then
    executor:submit("Ability Name", target_or_nil, {
      idempotencyKey = "route-action",
    })
  end
end)
Useful methods are new, tick, submit, can_replace, replace, cancel, has_pending, and status. Keep exactly one executor at the top-level rotation and pass it to sub-routes. idempotencyKey belongs to the helper, not the native gos.abilities.cast options table. The helper preserves pending ownership even when a busy result returns an existing command handle. status() is the helper's last published observation; keep calling tick() to refresh it.

The default is no selected-target fallback. Omit target_fallback when target_or_nil is nil: passing even "none" in that case is invalid. expectedStartAt and timeout are legacy helper option names that are stripped before submission; the current helper does not use them to schedule or expire a command.

items.title: combat_events
items.text:
Owns one combat cursor for the importing script and provides target-scoped handlers:

local Combat = require("combat_events")

Combat.on_player("damage", function(event)
  gos.log.info("Player damage", event.amount or 0)
end)

Combat.on_current_target("ability_activate", function(event)
  gos.log.debug("Target activated", event.name or "unknown")
end)

Combat.on_ally("heal", function(event)
  gos.log.success("Ally healed", event.effective_amount or event.amount or 0)
end)

The handler name matches either event.kind or event.action. The module preserves event order and reports dropped records through the script log.

items.title: Event scopes are destinations
items.text:
Combat.on_player means events targeting the local player, not every event sourced by that player. on_current_target matches the destination against the current selected target; on_ally matches a currently resolved friendly destination other than the local player. For outgoing damage or historical identities, read gos.events.combat directly and compare source_handle. These handlers match an event's kind or action. Register handlers at load time; the module owns its polling callback.

The executor example above is an integration fragment: Settings, should_cast and target_or_nil are supplied by your script. See the complete example for a self-contained entry point.

items.title: Build beyond individual API calls
items.text: You are not restricted to copying fixed scripts. Use the supported Lua language and standard libraries to create your own state machines, parsers, priority selectors, caches, UI models and modules. Game access and file access still use the supported public interfaces.

items.title: Separate responsibilities
items.text:
A top-level script owns settings, activation and callbacks. Plain modules can transform copied data without registering callbacks. An event collector can maintain a bounded model. A presentation callback draws that prepared model. When commands are involved, exactly one top-level executor owns them and is passed to routes.

A small project can consist of an entry point in the active scripts root and shared files such as my_tool_model.lua and my_tool_format.lua in the approved common root. Load them with require("my_tool_model"). Module state is cached per top-level script environment, not shared global state across every script.

items.title: Example: a plain Lua module
items.text:
-- my_tool_format.lua
local Format = {}
function Format.health(hp)
  if not hp or hp.percent == nil then return "unknown" end
  return string.format("%.0f%%", hp.percent)
end
return Format

Use it from another script:

local Format = require("my_tool_format")
gos.on_tick(function()
  local player = gos.world().player
  local text = Format.health(player and player:hp() or nil)
  -- Draw the prepared text or store it in your presentation model.
end, { interval_ms = 100 })

For histories, see the bounded ring-buffer module. Retain copied scalar data or opaque handles, not generation-bound world or unit objects.

items.title: Available facilities
items.text:
Base Lua, tables, strings, math, UTF-8 and coroutines are available. Time/date helpers and debug.traceback are exposed as described in runtime contracts. Coroutines are cooperative; they are not background threads and do not make blocking work safe.

Native module loading and unrestricted process access are not part of this environment. Use sandbox file helpers for permitted files and load-time resources. Package only the modules and assets your script needs; do not ask readers to copy your entire development workspace.

items.title: Keep each update finite
items.text:
Read one current world per callback. Prefer the player or selected target when that is all you need. Filter a unit query once and process a fixed maximum number of rows appropriate to the tool. Avoid nested all-unit scans and sorting the same unchanged data on every tick.

Use interval_ms for display work that does not need every update. A 100 ms status-panel cadence is a sample choice, not a universal recommendation. Input-edge handling may need every update; keep it small. Events and commands also have their own latency requirements.

items.title: Consume new events, not old history
items.text:
Retain the combat cursor, process only returned records, and cap the number of batches per callback. Each call yields at most 64 events. If more remains true, leave the rest for a later update. Track dropped; incomplete input must not look like a complete fight.

The incoming damage example uses at most four batches and keeps totals rather than storing every hit. A graph needs a fixed-capacity buffer or fixed time buckets. Never grow one table for an entire session without an eviction policy.

items.title: Prepare, then draw
items.text:
Maintain a small model and render from it. Use stable short drawing IDs so an update replaces an existing element. Use retained frame=true drawings for current callback output, and TTL drawings for intentionally persistent markers. Do not use long TTLs to disguise stale gameplay data.

The documented limits are ceilings, not performance targets: at most 192 frame commands from one callback and 512 active drawing commands overall, with at most 32 callback owners retaining frame output. Replacement uses the same owner, target, draw kind and bounded ID, not the ID alone. Share the available budget with other scripts.

items.title: Avoid expensive work in ticks
items.text:
Do not download, unzip, read or write files, rebuild lookup maps, emit per-event logs, or run blocking loops inside frequent callbacks. Prepare static data at load time. Log meaningful transitions with a bounded rate; store totals in memory instead of writing every observation.

Measure the tool in the real runtime with representative entity and event counts. A successful website build or an offline example check is not a game-performance test.

items.title: Runtime and data contracts
items.text:
Scripts run in isolated Lua environments on Core's update cadence. Register work with gos.on_tick; do not create a render loop or blocking loop.

The global gos table and its child tables are read-only. Standard Lua base, table, string, math, UTF-8, and coroutine facilities are available, together with os.clock, os.date, os.difftime, os.time, and debug.traceback. Process execution, unrestricted operating-system access, bytecode loading, and native modules are unavailable.

Conventions used throughout the API:

  • nil means the current snapshot does not contain that optional value.
  • Tables with status must be checked before their payload is used.
  • Ability, unit, effect, and command handles are opaque strings. Compare them or pass them back to Core; do not parse or persist them across game sessions.
  • Ability cooldowns, cast times, effect timers, and overlay TTL values use seconds.
  • gos.time_ms(), event timestamp, result wait_ms, and effect age_ms use milliseconds.
  • unit:distance() returns game-world coordinate units (multiply by 10 for metres) when both the local player and unit have a current matched spatial sample; otherwise it returns nil.
  • unit:position() uses game-world coordinate units and returns nil when the current prepared snapshot has no matched spatial sample for that unit.
  • unit:velocity() uses game-world coordinate units.
  • A GosWorld and its GosUnit values belong to one update generation. Store a unit handle, not the userdata, when identity must survive into a later tick.
  • Missing or pending data is not equivalent to zero, false, or absence.

items.title: Link directly to the relevant contract
items.text:
Open the API entry or guide, select the heading link, and copy its URL into your forum post. Each callable has a stable page. Search can find names such as gos.abilities.cast, definition_key, or incoming damage.

A useful question includes the observed behavior, the expected behavior, the relevant public API entry, and a short reproducible Lua snippet. State which observations were pending, unavailable or truncated. Do not present a queue result as confirmed activation.
path: Share scripts and ask useful questions

items.title: Keep reports minimal and private
items.text: Share only the snippet and public result fields needed to explain the problem. Remove account identifiers, character names, credentials, absolute personal paths and unrelated logs. Do not post a whole development folder, a full object dump, or files whose contents you have not reviewed. Unknown diagnostic fields are not needed to write a public script.
path: Share scripts and ask useful questions

items.title: Contribute more than reference entries
items.text: Examples, explanations of data availability, bounded data structures, UI patterns and module organization are all useful documentation contributions. Label fragments versus complete scripts, list required helper modules, and distinguish static review from in-game testing.
